predecessors.note: Mikawa, where Matsudaira Motoyasu (later Tokugawa Ieyasu), an Imagawa retainer (Okehazama page), 'openly ended his allegiance to the Imagawa clan and captured Kaminogō castle' in 1561 (Ieyasu page). Cliopatria's Warring States Japan row draws all Japan as one shape; the daimyo domains are internal units.

successors.note: Sekigahara and Ieyasu's seizure of power in 1600 (Ieyasu page); he was appointed shogun in 1603. The Tokugawa Shogunate row opens in October 1600.

capitals.name: Hamamatsu Castle
capitals.note: 'In 1570, Ieyasu established Hamamatsu as the capital of his territory.' The page does not say when he left it; 1590 is the move to the Kantō. The coordinates are the researcher's placement.

capitals.name: Edo Castle
capitals.note: He 'built his castle in the fishing village of Edo' after being relocated to the Kantō under Toyotomi; the page gives no year. 1590 is bridged from the Odawara siege. The coordinates are the researcher's placement.

rulers.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu (Matsudaira Motoyasu)
rulers.title: daimyō
rulers.note: Used the name Tokugawa from 1567 (clan page); seized power in 1600 and became shogun in 1603 (infobox 24 March 1603 to 16 April 1605); died 1 June 1616 at Sunpu.

correction.text: Kaminogō and the Okazaki area of Mikawa

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for a daimyo domain Cliopatria lacks (Warring States Japan draws all of Japan as one shape). 1561: Motoyasu 'openly ended his allegiance to the Imagawa clan and captured Kaminogō castle' (the clan page dates the declaration of independence to 1566 and the founding of the Tokugawa name to 1567). A 20 km circle (about 1,300 km2) stands for the first holding; the pages name no province for Kaminogō.
'By 1565, Ieyasu had become the master of all of Mikawa Province' (page marks the sentence citation needed). Eastern Aichi (12 cells, about 3,000 km2) stands for Mikawa.

1568-1569: Horikawa Castle in Tōtōmi besieged and captured; 1570 Hamamatsu the capital. A 40 km circle at Hamamatsu (about 5,100 km2) stands for Tōtōmi; the page does not call the province fully conquered. 25 January 1573: Mikatagahara in Tōtōmi, a Takeda victory; the Takeda took Yoshida and Futamata but the page does not say they held them.
1574: Katsuyori 'captured Takatenjin castle' (Katsuyori page); the Tokugawa lose it. A 25 km circle at Takatenjin is cut from the Tōtōmi circle.
1581: Ieyasu 'recapture[d] Takatenjin castle' (Ieyasu page); Katsuyori 'lost Takatenjin fortress to Tokugawa Ieyasu' (Katsuyori page).

union.text: southern Shinano: the part of Nagano Prefecture within 60 km of 35.95 N 138.0 E ('much of' Shinano)

correction.text: Mikawa, Tōtōmi, Suruga, Kai and southern Shinano: the five old provinces

keyframe_review.note: 1582: 'Nobunaga gave Ieyasu the right to govern Suruga Province' after the Takeda collapse (Ieyasu page); Tenshō-Jingo war: 'Tokugawa Ieyasu gained much of Kai Province and Shinano Province' (Sengoku page). The page puts the war among the Hōjō, Uesugi and Tokugawa over Shinano, Kōzuke and Kai. Yamanashi is Kai; the southern 39 cells of Nagano stand for 'much of' Shinano; the pages give no map. The five provinces are the researcher's name for these holdings (the Ieyasu page does not use 'five provinces').

union.text: Shimōsa and Kazusa, northern and central Chiba

correction.text: the five Hōjō provinces 'Sagami, Izu, Musashi, Shimosa, and Kazusa', given to Ieyasu in 1590

keyframe_review.note: Under Toyotomi 'Ieyasu was relocated to the Kanto plains' and 'built his castle in the fishing village of Edo' (Ieyasu page, no year); the Odawara page: 'Ieyasu was given the Hōjō lands' after the siege ended on 4 August 1590 (no provinces or koku). The Hōjō dossier's five provinces stand for them. The 1598 survey puts 2.5 million of 18.5 million koku in Ieyasu's hands (Azuchi–Momoyama page). Sekigahara (1600) ends this state.

region.text: Kaminogō and the Okazaki area of Mikawa

ledger.note: 1561: 'he openly ended his allegiance to the Imagawa clan and captured Kaminogō castle.' The Tokugawa clan page gives 1566 for the declaration of independence and 1567 for the Tokugawa name (infobox founding); the Okehazama page has Motoyasu pledge fealty to Oda after June 1560 and does not mention Okazaki.

minus.text: Kaminogō and the Okazaki area of Mikawa

ledger.note: By 1565: 'Ieyasu had become the master of all of Mikawa Province' (citation needed on the page). Mikawa had been Imagawa ground since Yoshimoto's advance; the Imagawa dossier carries the mirror loss.

1568-1569: 'Ieyasu besieged the Horikawa Castle in Tōtōmi' in 1568 and captured it in 1569; 1570 Hamamatsu is the capital. In 1567 Shingen and Ieyasu had 'occupied former Imagawa territory' (Shingen page). The page does not describe Tōtōmi as fully conquered.

1572: Shingen's move against Futamata and Hamamatsu; 'Shingen later captured Tokugawa's Futamata Castle'. 25 January 1573: Mikatagahara, a Takeda victory (the Ieyasu page puts the battle 'early in 1573').

1574: Katsuyori 'captured Takatenjin castle, which even his father had not managed to do'. The page names no province or previous holder; the Ieyasu page places the Tokugawa fortress-building around it in 1580.

1581: Ieyasu 'recapture[d] Takatenjin castle' after building fortresses to isolate it in 1580; Katsuyori 'lost Takatenjin fortress to Tokugawa Ieyasu, and 680 men of Okabe Motonobu's garrison died in the siege'.
1581: the Tōtōmi front closes with the loss of Takatenjin; the page gives no peace.

1582: 'Nobunaga gave Ieyasu the right to govern Suruga Province' after the Takeda collapse (the page: Nobunaga had assigned him control of Suruga around 1572 or 1573). Suruga had been Takeda land since 1569 (Takeda dossier).

union.text: southern Shinano: the part of Nagano Prefecture within 60 km of 35.95 N 138.0 E ('much of' Shinano)

ledger.note: 1582: the Tenshō-Jingo war; 'Tokugawa Ieyasu gained much of Kai Province and Shinano Province' (Sengoku page). The Nobunaga page credits Nobutada and Ieyasu with the conquest of Shinano and Kai in March 1582 (Oda dossier). The pages give no month or division.

ledger.note: 1600: 'After Hideyoshi's death and the Battle of Sekigahara, Ieyasu seized power in 1600' (Ieyasu page); the Sengoku page: the Eastern Army under Ieyasu defeated the Western Army. Appointed shogun in 1603. The Tokugawa Shogunate row opens in October 1600; the month is the row's, not the page's.

wars.name: Battle of Mikatagahara
wars.outcome: Takeda victory on 25 January 1573 north of Hamamatsu; the Tokugawa-Oda force 'almost totally annihilated'; Shingen withdrew and died in May 1573.
wars.note: Mirror of the Takeda dossier's 'Battle of Mikatagahara and the Mikawa campaign'.

wars.name: Battle of Nagashino
wars.outcome: The Oda-Tokugawa force (38,000) won a great victory over Katsuyori; no land changed at once.

wars.name: Siege of Takatenjin
wars.outcome: Ieyasu built fortresses to isolate the castle in 1580 and recaptured it in 1581.

wars.name: Tenshō-Jingo War

union.text: southern Shinano: the part of Nagano Prefecture within 60 km of 35.95 N 138.0 E ('much of' Shinano)

wars.outcome: A triangular conflict over Shinano, Kōzuke and Kai; Ieyasu gained much of Kai and Shinano.
wars.note: The Tenshō-Jingo page did not load; the Ieyasu and Sengoku pages are cited. The Ieyasu page's gloss that Kai is 'currently Gunma Prefecture' conflicts with its Suwamachi reference to Yamanashi.

wars.name: Battle of Komaki and Nagakute
wars.outcome: Inconclusive against Hideyoshi; no territory change on the pages.
wars.note: The Ieyasu page dates the fighting 1584 in one section and cites a source that gives 1582.

wars.name: Sekigahara campaign
wars.outcome: The Eastern Army under Ieyasu defeated the Western Army of Toyotomi loyalists; Ieyasu seized power in 1600.
wars.note: No province named on the pages.

certainty.note: The pages name castles and provinces, not borders; the Mikawa, Tōtōmi, Suruga, Kai and Shinano shapes are circles and prefectures.

sources.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu
sources.note: 1561 openly ended allegiance to the Imagawa and captured Kaminogo castle; by 1565 master of all Mikawa (citation needed); 1568 Horikawa in Totomi besieged, captured 1569; 1570 Hamamatsu capital; Nagashino 1575; 1581 recaptured Takatenjin; 1582 right to govern Suruga; Tensho-Jingo war over Shinano, Kozuke and Kai; Komaki-Nagakute 1584; relocated to the Kanto plains under Toyotomi, built his castle at Edo (no year); 1600 seized power; shogun 1603; died 1 June 1616 at Sunpu.

sources.title: Tokugawa clan
sources.note: Home province Mikawa; founded 1567 (Tokugawa name); 1566 declared independence from the Imagawa and reformed Mikawa; shogunate 1603-1868; Gosanke fiefs in Owari, Kishu and Mito.

sources.title: Battle of Mikatagahara
sources.note: 25 January 1573 in Totomi, north of Hamamatsu; Takeda victory; the Takeda captured Yoshida and Futamata Castles; Shingen did not intend to seize Hamamatsu and died in May 1573.

sources.title: Battle of Okehazama
sources.note: 12 June 1560 in Owari; Oda defeated the Imagawa; Matsudaira Motoyasu, an Imagawa retainer, pledged fealty to Oda; the Imagawa weakened and soon destroyed by neighbours.

sources.title: Sengoku period
sources.note: 1575 Nagashino; 1582 Tokugawa Ieyasu gained much of Kai and Shinano in the Tensho-Jingo war; 1590 Odawara; 1600 Sekigahara, the Eastern Army under Ieyasu defeats the Western Army.

sources.title: Siege of Odawara (1590)
sources.note: May to 4 August 1590; Ieyasu was given the Hojo lands (no provinces or koku on the page).

sources.title: Takeda Katsuyori
sources.note: 1574 Katsuyori captured Takatenjin; 1581 lost Takatenjin to Tokugawa Ieyasu; 2 March 1582 Takato lost; 11 March 1582 Tenmokuzan.

sources.title: Takeda Shingen
sources.note: 1567 Shingen and Ieyasu came to terms and occupied former Imagawa territory; 1572 Futamata.

sources.title: Azuchi–Momoyama period
sources.note: 1598 survey: 18.5 million koku nationally, 2.5 million in the hands of Ieyasu, whom Hideyoshi had moved to the Kanto; Komaki and Nagakute 1584; Nagashino 1575.

notes: Written by jk-01-x on 2026-10-19 from nine pages (Tokugawa Ieyasu, Tokugawa clan, Battle of Mikatagahara, Battle of Okehazama, Sengoku period, Siege of Odawara (1590), Takeda Katsuyori, Takeda Shingen, Azuchi–Momoyama period). The pre-shogunate Tokugawa as a Sengoku daimyo domain inside Cliopatria's single Warring States Japan row; it closes into the Tokugawa Shogunate row (opening October 1600). Dated by the pages: Mikawa (1561 first castle, 1565 'all of Mikawa'), Tōtōmi (1569), Takatenjin (lost 1574, regained 1581), Suruga (1582), Kai and much of Shinano (1582), the Kantō (1590). Page conflicts: the Ieyasu page puts the break with the Imagawa in 1561, the Tokugawa clan page in 1566 and the Tokugawa name in 1567; the Ieyasu page says Mikatagahara was early 1573, the Mikatagahara page 25 January 1573; the Ieyasu page puts Komaki-Nagakute in 1584 and 1582 in two places; its Kai gloss ('currently Gunma Prefecture') is wrong. Not on the pages: the five-provinces framing, the 1590 date of the transfer, the receivers of the five old provinces, the Kōzuke holding of 1582, koku totals, the Kiyosu alliance year, the Tenshō-Jingo settlement date (the Tenshō-Jingo War page did not load under two URL forms). Counterparts: 'imagawa-clan' (dossier written in this batch), 'takeda-clan', 'later-hojo-clan', 'uesugi-clan', 'oda-clan', 'toyotomi-clan' and 'tokugawa-shogunate' exist. The Toyotomi dossier carries the Hōjō lands as a vassal tint for this state from 1590 (not in its own shape). Area comparison not applicable (no infobox area).
